html:
The Treaty of Kyakhta, signed in 1727 at the border town of Kyakhta south of Lake Baikal, set the border between Russia and Qing China across Mongolia and fixed the rules for trade between them.

It built on the Treaty of Nerchinsk of 1689, which had settled the eastern part of the border. Kyakhta drew the line further west, through the lands of the Khalkha Mongols, now part of Mongolia. It also let a Russian Orthodox mission and language students stay in Beijing.

Trade was limited to a few border points, and Kyakhta became the main one. Russian furs went south; Chinese silk and above all tea came north on camel caravans across the Gobi, then on through Siberia. This Tea Road made Kyakhta rich. Together the two treaties shaped relations between Russia and China until the mid 1800s.
